name: Sam Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, how did you end up in this job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My uncle drove for the co-op dairy, and I used to ride in his cab in the school holidays. I got my car licence at 17, did the big truck licence at 21 with a loan from him, and I've been on the supermarket night run for six years now. It's steady, it's union, and the night premium is why I've got money in the bank.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I clock in at ten at night and back a 44-tonne fridge trailer into bays behind town-centre shops. Nobody has built a robot that can do that yet. I start at the distribution centre on the ring road and do three or four store drops before dawn. I like the empty roads and the radio, and the store lads usually have the kettle on. What wears me out is how tight those bays are, and sleeping in the day when the neighbours are mowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the stuff on the news is mostly sales talk. The trucks still need someone in the seat and someone to back them into a bay the width of a fridge. At the depot we'd probably laugh about it over the vending machine coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it would mean my life stays the same, and my life is fine. I've got about ten months of money saved, my partner Lena works as a nurse, and the depot is always short of drivers. The only thing that bugs me is the night shifts wearing me down, and AI wasn't going to fix that anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the night run and keep putting four hundred a month into the savings account, like now. Maybe I'd finally put in for a day route when one comes up, because Lena and I barely see each other on weekdays. I wouldn't touch any of the AI apps; I don't use them now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed, mostly. It's the world I already know. If anything I'd feel a bit smug, because my mates who keep saying trucks will drive themselves next year would have to buy me a drink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the night shifts wear you down. What does that look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Lena and I barely see each other on weekdays, and no robot story is going to fix my night shifts. Lena does early shifts at the hospital, so some weeks we only see each other at the kitchen table at seven in the morning, her with toast and me with a beer. We've talked about kids in a few years, and I can't picture doing nights with a baby. So the day route matters more to me than any robot story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything AI would take over in your day, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The route sheet maybe, and the paperwork for the temperature logs. The office already sends the drops to a tablet in the cab. If a computer sorted the order of the stops better, fine, as long as it doesn't tell me to park somewhere stupid.

say: I'd tell people the self-driving truck talk is **mostly sales hype**.
I'd point out that someone still has to **back an artic** into a tiny town-centre bay.
think: Privately I think my life simply **stays the same**, and that suits me fine.
My real worry is the **night shifts**, not AI, because Lena and I hardly see each other.
do: Keep doing the night supermarket run and putting **£400 a month** into savings.
Put in for a **day route** when one opens, so home life with Lena gets easier.
Stay away from **AI apps** completely, same as now.
feel: Relaxed and a little **smug** about the friends who predicted driverless trucks.
S0.quote: My partner Lena and I barely see each other on weekdays, and no robot story is going to fix my night shifts.
fieldNote: Sam's real pressure is **night work** and its strain on his relationship, not technology.
He has a strong cushion and a short driver queue at his depot, so his **income feels secure**.
He refuses AI tools on principle but accepts **software routing** that already arrives on his cab tablet.

steps.text: Keep the night supermarket run and save £400 a month
Bid for the next day route at the ring road depot
Top up the savings account toward a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that the office is going to get hit before we do, and we should look out for the planners. The drivers would be fine for a while, because nobody has built a robot that can chain a trailer or deal with a broken bay door at 3 a.m. Online I'd share the union stuff about protecting staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the people in the transport office are in trouble and the drivers are next in line, just later. If software does the booking and the planning, the company will want the truck itself to need fewer of us. I'm fine for a few years, but I don't like seeing the shape of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get more active in the union branch at the depot, go to the meetings instead of just paying the subs. I'd ask the rep, Dev, to push for a written deal that nobody loses their job to new tech without retraining. Money-wise I'd keep saving as normal, because my pay wouldn't change yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing a storm on the far side of the valley. It isn't on me yet, but I keep checking the sky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our shift planner Maureen has done the rota for twenty years. If a computer takes over the rota, she's out at 58. Maureen knows which store manager will scream if the bread is late, and losing her would make me sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stick with paper and your own head. Would the company let you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not forever. They'd make us use whatever app they buy, and I'd use it because I have to, the way I use the cab tablet now. But I won't go home and play with chatbots in my free time; I'd rather fix my bike.

say: I'd warn workmates that the **transport office** gets hit before the drivers do.
I'd share **union posts** online about protecting staff when new tech comes in.
think: Privately I think drivers are **next in line**, just a few years behind the planners.
My own **pay stays safe** for now, but I don't like where it's heading.
do: Go to the **union branch meetings** at the depot instead of just paying subs.
Ask Dev, the rep, to push for a **written no-redundancy deal** tied to retraining.
Keep saving as usual, because my **pay** wouldn't change yet.
feel: **Uneasy**, like watching a storm on the far side of the valley.
S1.quote: Our shift planner Maureen has done the rota for twenty years. If a computer takes over the rota, she's out at 58.
fieldNote: Sam's first concern is for **older office staff**, which fits his pro-union outlook.
He sees drivers as **protected for now** because his work is hands-on and messy.
He will use **company apps** when forced but refuses AI in his own time.

steps.text: Attend every union branch meeting at the depot this year
Ask the union rep for a written no-redundancy tech deal
Keep the night run and the usual monthly savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws before the companies get their hands on it. At work I'd be loud about it: the union needs to fight now, not in 2031 when the robot trucks roll out. Online I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my driving job is gone by the time I'm 32. The planning office goes in 2028, and then three years later a robot does what I do. My savings would last most of a year, but every driver in the country would be looking for work at the same time, so 'plenty of jobs nearby' means nothing then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop the house-deposit plan and keep the money liquid, and I'd cut the holiday Lena and I had booked. I'd push the union to get a deal for drivers, like guaranteed pay or retraining money before the robots arrive. And I'd vote for whoever promises to tax the companies running robot fleets and put the money back to workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, if I'm honest. Lena keeps telling me nurses will be fine, and I'm glad. My driving job is gone by the time I'm 32, and I don't want to be the guy at home living off my partner's nurse wage. I'd be lying awake on my days off, which is saying something for a night worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between AGI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They mean I'd watch it coming. The office gets wiped out first, then they'd trial driverless trucks on the motorway at night, which is exactly my run. Three years is enough time to be scared, but I don't know what I'd train for that robots wouldn't also do by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're not buying the house yet and we're not having a baby yet, not until I know what I'm doing for money. She'd say that's me being dramatic. Maybe, but I'd rather be dramatic than broke.

say: I'd demand **laws** on robot trucks before the companies roll them out.
I'd tell the union to **fight now**, not in 2031 when trucks drive themselves.
think: Privately I think my **driving job is gone** by the time I'm 32.
Every driver would be job hunting at once, so **plenty of local jobs** would mean nothing.
do: Pause the **house deposit** and keep the savings in cash.
Cancel the booked **holiday** with Lena to stretch the money.
Push the union and vote for a **robot-fleet tax** that funds displaced drivers.
feel: **Sick** and sleepless, and ashamed at the thought of living off **Lena's wage**.
S2.quote: My driving job is gone by the time I'm 32, and I don't want to be the guy at home living off my partner's nurse wage.
fieldNote: Sam expects to **lose his job** and treats the three-year robot gap as only time to worry.
His strong savings help, but he thinks **every driver** would compete for the same work.
He puts **family plans** on hold, including the house and a baby.

steps.text: Pause the house deposit plan and keep savings in cash
Cancel the booked holiday with Lena this year
Push the depot union for paid retraining before robot trucks
Vote for parties promising a tax on robot truck fleets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not a lot, so the union and the government need to get moving. At work I'd keep it practical: the routing and booking change first, then the trucks. I'd tell the younger drivers not to buy expensive cars on finance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending, just with time to see it. The thinking side of the job, which is barely anything for me, changes in 2031, and the trucks go driverless around 2034, when I'm 35. Five years is time to save, but I'm not someone who switches careers easily. I don't know what to fill the gap with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and keep saving, but harder, maybe six hundred a month instead of four. I'd go to the union's national conference, not just the branch, because this would be the big fight. I'd vote with that in mind at the next election too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not panicking. There's a gap to work with. I just don't like the blank where the plan should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't switch easily. What's one thing you might actually try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the forklift and yard work at the depot, because someone still has to shunt trailers when things go wrong. Or truck maintenance, because I like fixing my bike. But robots would come for the yard too, wouldn't they?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if you wanted to save more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second-hand motorbike I've been eyeing. I've had the money for it since summer. In this picture I'd leave it in the bank.

say: I'd say five years is **not a lot** and the government has to move.
I'd warn younger drivers off buying **cars on finance**.
think: Privately it's the **same ending** with more time to watch it coming.
My trucks go driverless around **2034**, when I'm 35, and I'm slow to change careers.
do: Raise savings from **£400 to £600** a month while still driving.
Go to the union's **national conference** to push for driver protections.
Skip buying the **second-hand motorbike** and leave that money banked.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicking, because there's a gap to work with.
S3.quote: Five years is time to save, but I'm not someone who switches careers easily. I don't know what to fill the gap with.
fieldNote: Sam knows his job is **mostly hands-on**, so AGI barely touches him until robots arrive.
His resistance shows as not knowing **what to train for**, rather than denial.
He turns to **union activity** and saving rather than learning new tools.

steps.text: Attend the union's national conference on driverless trucks
Vote for candidates backing protections for professional drivers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, if the people in charge actually bother. I'd still be banging the union drum at work. I'd also tell people that it's 2039 before robots can do my job, so nobody should panic yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably sit on it longer than I should. Ten years feels like forever when you're 27. It's hard to change your life for something you can't see out of the windscreen. I'd be 40 when the robots came. I'd wait and see for a few years, then panic around year six. I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd carry on driving and keep up the union work. I'd probably sign up for the heavy vehicle mechanic evening course the college runs, because Lena would nag me until I did. Then I'd see how fast things moved before doing anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slow, background way. Like a dentist appointment far off in the calendar. I'd keep forgetting it and then remembering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd panic around year six. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because nothing would look different for years. The trucks would be the same, the stores would be the same, Dev would still be moaning about the canteen. Nothing would push me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about kids, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still have them, in maybe three years. Ten years means a child would be in school before the robots came. I'd want them to grow up knowing their dad had a plan, even if the plan is fixing trucks instead of driving them.

say: I'd tell people that robots can't do my job until **2039**, so nobody should panic.
I'd keep pushing the **union** to plan the change properly.
think: Privately I'd **sit on it** too long because ten years feels like forever at 27.
I'd probably wait, then **panic around year six**, because I know myself.
do: Keep driving the night run and keep up the **union work**.
Sign up for the college's **heavy vehicle mechanic** evening course.
Wait to see how fast **driverless trucks** spread before doing anything bigger.
feel: A slow, **background anxiety**, like a dentist appointment far off in the calendar.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like forever when you're 27. It's hard to change your life for something you can't see out of the windscreen.
fieldNote: Sam is honest that **more time** would make him delay, not plan.
The mechanic course is driven by **Lena's nagging**, not his own appetite for change.
He would still **have children**, because a decade feels long enough to adjust.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's heavy vehicle mechanic evening course
Keep up the union work on driverless truck rules
Watch driverless truck trials for a few years before deciding more

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Three years from robot brains to robot trucks is nothing, and I'd be 32 with no other trade. What would help is the union getting a real deal now: paid retraining, and a decent payout for drivers whose routes go driverless, funded by the companies that profit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who'd be on the roads with these robot trucks. I've seen what happens when a cyclist wobbles at night, and I want to know who answers for it when there's no driver. Nobody on the news ever asks that.

headlineQuote: I clock in at ten at night and back a 44-tonne fridge trailer into bays behind town-centre shops. Nobody has built a robot that can do that yet.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old** night driver on a unionised supermarket run, living with his partner Lena, a nurse.
He has about **ten months saved** and steady work, so AI Plateau and Steady Disruption barely shake him.
He refuses **AI tools** in his own life and turns to the **union** whenever change looms.
Fast AGI alarms him, because he expects **robot trucks** to take his job by 32.
With ten years he admits he'd **delay**, then start a mechanic course under pressure.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robot trucks would arrive when he's 32 with no other trade.
whatWouldHelp: A union deal for **paid retraining** and payouts, funded by the firms running **robot fleets**.
